items.title: Bark, bite or let sleeping dogs lie?
items.summary: Watchdog of the Constitution. Apex Ombudsman. Sentinel on the qui vive. Even as its monikers get more obscure, the role of the Supreme Court of India as the final protector of our rights has always been clear. That the Court has not always covered itself in glory while guarding the house we live in is, in its own words, a shame that deserves to be buried ten fathoms deep . Amidst reluctant whispers of the 'E' word (Emergency Lite, if you will) today, its ears surely must prick up. The mantle that rests on its shoulders, its own former members would say, has never weighed heavier in recent times than now. On October 15, the apex watchdog will hear a number of matters on protests related to the functioning of the Election Commission of India (ECI), the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, voter deletions and the State's quelling of those same protests. At stake are a host of rights guaranteed under the Constitution of India, the very document the Supreme Court was formed to protect. items.title: Ten years without Najeeb: What happened to the ‘Idea of JNU’ and its promise of equality?
items.summary: On October 15, 2016, Najeeb Ahmed, a student at Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU), went missing. The disappearance came a day after an alleged altercation with members of the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP). In the days that followed, students demanded answers from the university administration and sought accountability for what had happened. A movement emerged around a question that should never have become so difficult to ask: Where is Najeeb? Ten years later, that question remains unanswered. The official investigation was closed after the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) filed its closure report, which a Delhi court accepted in June 2025. The Delhi High Court subsequently upheld the decision in December 2025 . The courts have not established what happened to Najeeb or where he is. But Najeeb's disappearance raises another question, one that concerns the political life of the university itself: whatever happened to the “Idea of JNU”? I witnessed the political life of JNU from mid-2015 onwards. A Bench of Justice JB Pardiwala and Justice K Vinod Chandran made the remarks while hearing a plea challenging a November 2024 judgment of the Chhattisgarh High Court. The High Court order had set aside a man's murder conviction and instead convicted him of culpable homicide not amounting to murder and sentenced him to 10 years in prison instead of life imprisonment. "Just see the pathetic condition of the High Court. The judges don’t know what is Section 304 part I (culpable homicide not amounting to murder involving intention to cause death or likely-fatal injury) and Section 304 Part II IPC (culpable homicide not amounting to murder involving knowledge that the act is likely to cause death, but no such intention)! items.title: Three Malayalis killed in Germany apartment fire, suspect arrested
items.summary: Three Keralam natives were killed and five people injured in a fire at a residential building in Bochum, Germany, on Tuesday, October 14. Police have arrested a 41-year-old Romanian resident of the building on suspicion of murder. The deceased were identified as Anjali Sheela Joy from Kollam, Nova Sabu from Kattappana in Idukki, and Sivin Johny from Kalady in Ernakulam. They had moved into an apartment on the building’s second floor about two weeks before the fire. According to reports, the fire broke out at around 4.15 am in the multi-family building in Bochum’s Hofstede district. Firefighters found the three victims dead in their apartment. Flames and smoke spread through the stairwell, initially preventing emergency crew from reaching residents on the upper floors. Rescue teams evacuated four people using ladders, while another resident escaped onto an air cushion. Five people were injured, reportedly from smoke inhalation, and taken to hospital, reports said. While Anjali had moved to Germany for higher studies, Nova had moved there about six months ago for work. Sivin had arrived only around a fortnight before the fire to pursue higher studies. items.title: ‘Trivial punishment is not a criminal act’: Kerala HC quashes case against teacher accused of pulling student’s hand
items.summary: The Kerala High Court has quashed criminal proceedings against a teacher accused of physically pulling up a Class 5 student at a school in Thiruvalla, observing that the materials collected during the investigation did not indicate any criminal intention to harass, abuse or injure the child. Justice Jobin Sebastian, in an order dated October 9, 2026, said a teacher cannot be prosecuted merely for imposing a trivial punishment as a corrective measure to maintain discipline in an educational institution, provided it is not inflicted with malicious intent. The court was hearing a petition filed by Jolly John, a former class teacher of Standard V-C at MGM School, Thiruvalla, seeking to quash the final report in a case registered by the Thiruvalla police in 2019 and the subsequent proceedings before the Additional Sessions Court-I, Pathanamthitta. The teacher was accused of catching hold of a fifth-standard student's hand and pulling her up on December 6, 2018, at around 3.30 pm. According to the prosecution, the child's leg got entangled in a bench during the incident, causing a contusion and pain in her right knee.
